lesson.subtitle: Lesson 1 -- The Clause That Broke
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Inês (Mock TBL) | Lesson 1 -- The Clause That Broke

paras: In cross-border deals, the clause that causes the most litigation is rarely the one the parties argued about. It is the earn-out: the part of the price that the seller only receives if the business hits certain targets after closing. On paper it looks like a fair compromise, and it is often sold to the seller as a vote of confidence. In practice it hands the buyer control of the very numbers that determine what the seller gets paid.

A common pattern goes like this. The seller accepts a lower headline price in exchange for an earn-out worth thirty per cent of the total. The buyer, now running the company, decides to invest heavily in a new market. The investment is defensible, even sensible, and it depresses profit for exactly the two years the earn-out is measured over. The seller receives nothing, and nothing improper has happened. There is no bad faith to point at, no clause that was broken, and therefore very little to litigate.

Experienced counsel therefore stop negotiating the number and start negotiating the definitions. What counts as profit. Whether central overheads allocated from the parent company are deducted before the calculation. Who prepares the accounts, and what happens if the seller disagrees with them. Whether the buyer owes any duty to operate the business so as to give the earn-out a fair chance. English courts have been reluctant to imply that duty where the contract is silent, which means silence is a choice with consequences.

There is a second trap that arrives later. Even where the definitions are tight, the seller usually has no mechanism to see the workings. A clause that promises audited accounts within ninety days is worth little if the seller cannot ask a question about how a line was built. Practitioners who have lived through one of these disputes tend to insist on two unglamorous things: an independent expert named in advance, and a right of access to the underlying records, exercisable without a court.

The practical lesson is uncomfortable, because it asks the party with less power to spend what little leverage it has on something that feels procedural. In an earn-out, that party should spend its remaining leverage not on price, but on the machinery that measures performance. Ask who holds the pen after closing. Ask who checks the arithmetic, and who pays for the check. Whatever the answers are, write them down.

language.title: Reveal answer key
list: They keep the conversation open: probing, conceding conditionally, signalling disagreement before making it, testing the downside.
Because it names the thing you will give up, which makes the thing you are asking for sound like the small ask — and it moves the negotiation off price, where you cannot win.
Open answer — most counsel would not park a point in front of their own client, because it reads as indecision rather than tactics.

items: The situation — you act for the seller

The buyer's draft has landed: headline price 18% below the original offer · an earn-out worth 30% of the total · measured on EBITDA over two years · accounts prepared by the buyer · no operating covenants · no independent expert named. Your teacher is Mr Hall, counsel for the buyer.
Plan first — 2 minutes, out loud

Before you speak to Mr Hall: which three points will you open with, and in what order? Say them out loud. You may not simply demand a higher price — if you go there, Mr Hall will accept, and the earn-out protections go with it.
Then negotiate — the tangible outcome
By the end you and Mr Hall must have agreed OUT LOUD on three things: (1) who prepares the accounts, (2) one definition you have changed and how, and (3) what happens if the buyer opens a new market.
Report — back to your client, alone

Now your teacher stops being Mr Hall. In 90 seconds, uninterrupted, report what you agreed: the three points, what you gave up to get each one, and the one risk that is still open. Nobody will help you and nobody will interrupt.

task1.title: What the report has to contain
items: The three agreements, in the order that matters to your client — not the order they happened in.
What you traded for each one. If you got something for nothing, say so.
The risk you did NOT close, named plainly and without hedging.
What you need from your client to move: a decision, a date, or a number.

task1.label: Useful language
items: I'd want to understand what sits behind that number.
That's workable in principle, provided that...
Let me push back on one thing.
Where does that leave my client if...?
I can live with the number if we fix the definition.
We could move on that, but I'd need something back.
Can we park that and come back to it?
On that basis, yes.
The situation

Different task, same theme, and it does not depend on how the negotiation ended. Mr Hall's client will not move on the accounts point. Your client is on the phone with sixty seconds and one question: sign, or walk?
The three options on the table

(1) Sign as it stands and accept the risk. (2) Walk away and go back to the second bidder, who offered less cash but no earn-out. (3) Sign, but only with an independent expert on the accounts — which means another two weeks and a buyer who may lose patience.

task2.title: What your client needs, in this order
items: The recommendation — one of the three, in your first sentence. Not a summary of the options.
The reason, compressed into one sentence she can repeat to her board.
The risk you are asking her to accept, named out loud. Not hedged.
What you need from her to move.

task2.text: Your teacher will take the opposite view and give you one hard objection. Hold the recommendation or change it — either is fine, as long as the reason changes with it.

wrapup.title: Wrap-up
items: In one sentence: what does a seller trade in an earn-out, and what should they buy with it?
Which of the twelve expressions will you use in a real call this month?
Was there a moment today when you said yes because the English ran out, not because you agreed?
